paragraphs.heading: Oldest at the bottom
paragraphs.text: The law of superposition is one of the base principles of geology, paleontology and other fields that deal with geological stratigraphy. Put simply, in a sequence of layers that has not been deformed, the oldest layers lie at the bottom, and newer material piles up on top over time. Stratigraphic dating depends on this law holding true, along with other assumptions, such as the idea that an object cannot be older than the materials it is made of.

paragraphs.heading: Putting fossils in order
paragraphs.text: When sedimentary rock has been deformed by no more than 90°, its oldest layers still sit at the bottom. That lets paleontologists and paleobotanists rank the relative ages of fossils found in the layers, with the remains of the most archaic lifeforms in the lowest ones. Such findings show which species lived at the same time and which came one after another, perhaps in an order that matters for evolution.

paragraphs.heading: Steno and Smith
paragraphs.text: The Danish scientist Nicolas Steno first proposed the law in 1669, as one of the main theses of his work Dissertationis prodromus. In English-language writing it was made popular by William "Strata" Smith, who used it to draw the first geologic map of Britain. It is the first of Smith's laws, formally published in Strata Identified by Fossils (1816–1819).

paragraphs.heading: A trickier rule in archaeology
paragraphs.text: Archaeologists use superposition a little differently, because people lay down layers in other ways than natural processes do. Human-made layers need not build up in time order from top to bottom. Some are made by cutting into older layers: the silt that back-fills an underground drain forms some time after the ground just above it. Changes to standing buildings, such as new doors and windows made in a wall, are another case, so reading the sequence calls for interpretation.

paragraphs.heading: When layers get mixed up
paragraphs.text: Even layers laid down by nature can later be disturbed or reshuffled by animals, plants and limestone crystallization. Layers formed at the surface by lava flows and ash falls also behave differently. Under certain conditions, then, superposition does not always apply.
